lessons.title: Introduction to Python
lessons.content: Python is a readable, general-purpose language used in web development, data science, automation and AI. Its clean syntax makes it a common first language.
lessons.notes: Python code runs top to bottom, using indentation instead of braces to define blocks.
lessons.mistakes: Mixing tabs and spaces for indentation causes errors.
lessons.practice: Predict the output of print("Hello WaiTech") before checking.
lessons.challenge: Print your name and the language you're learning in two separate print statements.

hint.en: Used in web, data, automation and AI.
hint.sw: Hutumika kwenye web, data, automation na AI.

explanation.en: Clean syntax makes it a common first language.
explanation.sw: Sintaksia safi huifanya iwe lugha ya kwanza maarufu.

explanation.en: print writes text to the screen.

hint.en: Many ML libraries are in Python.
hint.sw: Maktaba nyingi za ML ni za Python.

explanation.en: Python is popular for data and AI.
explanation.sw: Python ni maarufu kwa data na AI.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.content: Python variables don't require a declared type — the interpreter infers it from the assigned value, and the type can change as the program runs.
lessons.notes: Dynamic typing is flexible but requires discipline to avoid confusing bugs.
lessons.mistakes: Reassigning a variable to an unrelated type by accident.
lessons.practice: Assign a name and age variable, then print both.
lessons.challenge: Reassign the age variable and print it again.

quiz.question: Do you declare a type for a Python variable?

explanation.en: The interpreter infers the type from the value.
explanation.sw: Interpreter hubaini aina kutoka kwa thamani.

hint.en: print separates arguments with a space.

explanation.en: Multiple arguments are joined with spaces.

quiz.question: Can a variable change type later?

explanation.en: Python allows rebinding to any type.

lessons.title: Data Types
objectives: Identify str, int, float and bool
Use type() to check a value
lessons.content: Python's core built-in types include str (text), int (whole numbers), float (decimals) and bool (True/False).
lessons.notes: type() returns the exact class of a value, useful for debugging.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting that dividing two ints with / always returns a float in Python 3.
lessons.practice: Check the type of three different variables using type().
lessons.challenge: Convert a string number into an int using int().

lessons.title: Operators
lessons.content: Python supports standard arithmetic operators plus // for floor division and % for modulo (remainder), both common in beginner exercises.
lessons.notes: % is especially useful for checking even/odd numbers or cycling values.
lessons.practice: Use % to check if a number is even.
lessons.challenge: Use // to divide two numbers and print the whole-number result.

quiz.question: Which operator raises to a power?

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.content: f-strings (f"...") let you embed expressions directly inside string literals, similar to JavaScript template literals.
lessons.notes: f-strings are the modern, preferred way to format strings in Python.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting the f prefix, which causes the braces to print literally.
lessons.practice: Build a greeting using an f-string with a variable.
lessons.challenge: Use .upper() and .strip() on a sample string.

quiz.question: Which line is a valid f-string?

explanation.sw: upper() hurudisha nakala ya herufi kubwa.

lessons.title: Numbers
objectives: Work with int and float math
lessons.content: Python handles integer and floating point math natively, and the built-in round() function rounds to a given number of decimal places.
lessons.notes: round() uses banker's rounding on ties, which can surprise beginners.
lessons.practice: Round a price to two decimal places.
lessons.challenge: Calculate the average of three numbers and round the result.

explanation.en: The second argument is the number of decimals.
explanation.sw: Hoja ya pili ni idadi ya desimali.

quiz.question: Which function gives the absolute value?

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.content: Lists store ordered, changeable collections of items. Items are added with .append() and accessed using zero-based indexing.
lessons.notes: Negative indexes count from the end of the list, e.g. list[-1] is the last item.
lessons.mistakes: Trying to index past the end of a list, causing an IndexError.
lessons.practice: Create a list of three languages and print the last one using -1.
lessons.challenge: Append a new language and print the full list.

quiz.question: Which adds an item to the end?

explanation.en: append adds to the end of a list.

hint.en: You can append and edit items.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.content: Dictionaries store key-value pairs, similar to JavaScript objects. Keys must be unique, and values are accessed using square brackets.
lessons.notes: Since Python 3.7, dictionaries preserve insertion order.
lessons.mistakes: Accessing a missing key directly causes a KeyError — use .get() to avoid this.
lessons.practice: Create a learner dictionary with name, level and goal keys.
lessons.challenge: Use .get() to safely access a key that might not exist.

quiz.question: How do you read the name?

explanation.en: Dictionary values are read by key.
explanation.sw: Thamani za dictionary husomwa kwa key.

explanation.en: A key appears once; later assignment overwrites.
explanation.sw: Key hutokea mara moja; mgawo wa baadaye hubatilisha.

quiz.question: What does learner.get("age", 0) return if there is no age key?

hint.en: The second argument is the default.

explanation.en: get avoids KeyError and returns the default.
explanation.sw: get huepuka KeyError na hurudisha chaguo-msingi.

lessons.title: Conditions
lessons.content: Python conditionals use if, elif, and else, with indentation defining each block instead of braces.
lessons.notes: Consistent indentation (4 spaces is the convention) is required, not optional.
lessons.mistakes: Mixing indentation levels within the same block.
lessons.practice: Write an if/elif/else that grades a score into A, B, or C.
lessons.challenge: Combine two conditions with 'and' in a single if statement.

quiz.question: What does this print?
What defines a block in Python?

lessons.title: Loops
objectives: Write a for loop over a range
lessons.content: Python's for loop iterates directly over sequences — a range of numbers, a list, or a string — without needing a manual counter.
lessons.mistakes: Expecting range(5) to include the number 5.
lessons.practice: Loop through range(5) and print each number.
lessons.challenge: Loop through a list of languages and print each one.

quiz.question: Which loop runs over a list directly?
What does while do?
options: Repeats while a condition is true

explanation.en: while repeats until the condition is false.
explanation.sw: while hurudia hadi sharti liwe si kweli.

lessons.title: Functions & Parameters
lessons.content: Functions group reusable logic. Parameters can have default values, and functions return data using the return keyword.
lessons.notes: A function without an explicit return statement returns None.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting return and expecting the function's last expression to be the output.
lessons.practice: Write a function that greets a user with a default name.
lessons.challenge: Add a second parameter with its own default value.

quiz.question: Which keyword sends a value back?

hint.sw: Ni ya kawaida kwenye lugha nyingi.

explanation.en: return ends the function with a result.

quiz.question: What does a function without return give?

lessons.title: List Comprehensions
lessons.content: List comprehensions provide a compact way to build a new list from an existing iterable, optionally filtering with an if clause.
lessons.notes: Comprehensions are more Pythonic than manually appending inside a loop for simple transforms.
lessons.mistakes: Writing comprehensions so complex they become harder to read than a plain loop.
lessons.practice: Build a list of squares from 1 to 5 using a comprehension.
lessons.challenge: Add a filter so only even squares are included.
lessons.code:
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)

quiz.question: What does this return?
quiz.code: [n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]

quiz.question: Why use list comprehensions?
options: A compact way to build lists

explanation.en: They replace simple for loops that append.

lessons.title: Exceptions
lessons.content: try/except catches runtime errors so a program can fail gracefully instead of crashing, and specific exception types can be caught individually.
lessons.notes: Catching a bare 'except:' hides real bugs — catch specific exception types instead.
lessons.mistakes: Silently swallowing all exceptions without logging or handling them meaningfully.
lessons.practice: Wrap a division in try/except to catch a ZeroDivisionError.
lessons.challenge: Raise a custom ValueError with a descriptive message.

quiz.question: What does this print?

hint.en: Division by zero raises an error.

quiz.question: Why catch specific exceptions?
options: So you handle only what you expect

explanation.sw: Kukamata kila kitu huficha makosa halisi.

quiz.question: Which block runs only if no error happened?

lessons.title: Classes & Objects
objectives: Define a class with attributes and methods
lessons.content: Classes bundle data and behavior together. The __init__ method initializes new instances, and self refers to the current instance inside methods.
lessons.notes: self must be the first parameter of every instance method, by convention.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting self as the first parameter of a method definition.
lessons.practice: Define a Learner class with a name attribute and an introduce() method.
lessons.challenge: Add a second method that tracks completed lessons.

explanation.en: It runs when you create an object.
self gives access to instance data.
explanation.sw: self hutoa ufikiaji wa data ya instance.

quiz.question: What does Learner("Alex").introduce() return?

explanation.en: The method reads the stored name.

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.content: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another class's behavior. A subclass can override methods to customize behavior while keeping shared logic in the base class.
lessons.notes: super() calls the parent class's implementation, useful when extending rather than fully replacing behavior.
lessons.mistakes: Overusing inheritance for code reuse when composition would be simpler.
lessons.practice: Create a MentorLearner subclass that overrides introduce().
lessons.challenge: Call super().introduce() inside the overridden method.

explanation.sw: Subclass hutumia tabia ya base class.

explanation.en: It lets you extend rather than replace a method.
explanation.sw: Hukuruhusu kuongeza badala ya kubadilisha method.

quiz.question: What is overriding?
options: A subclass redefining a parent method

explanation.en: The subclass version is used instead.
explanation.sw: Toleo la subclass hutumika badala yake.

lessons.title: Writing Basic Tests
lessons.content: Automated tests verify your code behaves as expected as it grows. The built-in assert statement is the simplest starting point before adopting a framework like pytest.
lessons.notes: A failing assert raises an AssertionError, immediately signalling unexpected behavior.
lessons.mistakes: Only testing the 'happy path' and never checking edge cases like empty input.
lessons.practice: Write an assert statement verifying greet('Alex') returns the right string.
lessons.challenge: Add a second assert covering the default-parameter case.
lessons.code:
assert greet("Alex") == "Hello, Alex!"
assert greet() == "Hello, coder!"

quiz.question: What does assert do?
options: Raises an error if the condition is false

explanation.en: assert fails loudly when something is wrong.
explanation.sw: assert hushindwa kwa sauti kitu kikikosea.

hint.sw: Imepewa jina la majaribio ya Python.

explanation.en: pytest builds on simple assert statements.
explanation.sw: pytest hujengwa juu ya assert rahisi.
